content.title: 3. DIAGNOSTIC TESTING FOR PAD
section_headings: 3.1 Resting ABI and Additional Physiological Testing
content.narrative_summary: This section introduces diagnostic testing for suspected peripheral artery disease (PAD), emphasizing a multifaceted approach including history, physical examination, ankle–brachial index (ABI), additional physiological tests, noninvasive and invasive imaging, and the appropriate indications to guide resource utilization. It transitions to recommendations for resting and exercise ABI and other physiological assessments.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Resting ABI and Additional Physiological Testing

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with history or physical examination findings suggestive of PAD (Table 6), the resting ABI, with or without ankle pulse volume recordings (PVR) and/or Doppler waveforms, is recommended to establish the diagnosis.1,2
2. The resting ABI should be reported as abnormal (ABI ≤0.90), borderline (ABI 0.91-0.99), normal (ABI 1.00-1.40), or noncompressible (ABI >1.40).3
3. In patients at increased risk of PAD (Table 5), screening for PAD with the resting ABI, with or without ankle PVR and/or Doppler waveforms, is reasonable.4-9
4. In patients not at increased risk of PAD (Table 5) and without history or physical examination findings suggestive of PAD (Table 6), screening for PAD with the ABI is not recommended.10,11
5. In patients with suspected PAD, toe pressure/toe-brachial index (TBI) with waveforms should be performed when the resting ABI is >1.40 (noncompressible).12-17

6. Patients with suspected chronic symptomatic PAD (ie, exertional nonjoint-related leg symptoms) and normal or borderline resting ABI (>0.90 and ≤1.40, respectively) should undergo exercise treadmill ABI testing to evaluate for PAD.18,19
7. In patients with PAD and an abnormal resting ABI (≤0.90), the exercise treadmill ABI test can be useful to objectively assess the functional status and walking performance.20-25

8. In patients with chronic symptomatic PAD, it is reasonable to perform segmental leg pressures with PVR and/or Doppler waveforms in addition to the resting ABI to help delineate the anatomic level of PAD.26,27

9. In patients with suspected CLTI, it is reasonable to use toe pressure/TBI with waveforms, transcutaneous oxygen pressure (TcPO2), and/or skin perfusion pressure (SPP) in addition to ABI for assessment of arterial perfusion and to establish the diagnosis of CLTI.13,28-37

10. In patients with CLTI with nonhealing wounds or gangrene, it can be useful to use toe pressure/TBI with waveforms, TcPO2, SPP, and/or other local perfusion measures to determine the likelihood of wound healing without or after revascularization.13,14,28,33-36,38

content.title: 4.2. Health Disparities in PAD
section_headings: Recommendation for Health Disparities in PAD
content.narrative_summary: Synopsis: Disparities in the detection, management, and outcomes of PAD are longstanding in the United States, disproportionately affecting high-risk racial and ethnic groups, lower-socioeconomic-status patients, and rural residents. Structural determinants such as housing, health care access, education, income inequality, and structural racism contribute to higher rates of limb amputation, cardiovascular mortality, and stroke, particularly among Black Americans. Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text: Evidence of health disparities in PAD is common but may be difficult to discern. Patient-centered efforts include identifying disenfranchised at-risk populations by assessing symptoms such as exertional leg pain and impaired walking, conducting thorough physical examinations (including pulses and foot assessment), implementing comprehensive care plans with guideline-directed medical therapy and management of comorbidities, addressing socioeconomic and other barriers (see Sections 2.2, 5, 6, and 12), and ensuring longitudinal follow-up for disadvantaged patients to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and limb amputation.

content.title: Section 5.1. Antiplatelet and Antithrombotic Therapy for PAD
section_headings: 5.1. Antiplatelet and Antithrombotic Therapy for PAD
content.narrative_summary: A summary table of class of recommendation and level of evidence for antiplatelet and antithrombotic therapies in patients with peripheral artery disease.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Antiplatelet and Antithrombotic Therapy for PAD

rows.recommendation: In patients with symptomatic PAD, single antiplatelet therapy is recommended to reduce the risk of MACE.1-4
In patients with symptomatic PAD, single antiplatelet therapy with clopidogrel alone (75 mg daily) is recommended to reduce the risk of MACE.4
In patients with symptomatic PAD, single antiplatelet therapy with aspirin alone (range, 75–325 mg daily) is recommended to reduce the risk of MACE.1-3
In patients with symptomatic PAD, low-dose rivaroxaban (2.5 mg twice daily) combined with low-dose aspirin is effective to reduce the risk of MACE and MALE.5,6
After endovascular or surgical revascularization for PAD, antiplatelet therapy is recommended.1,7-9
After endovascular or surgical revascularization for PAD, low-dose rivaroxaban (2.5 mg twice daily) combined with low-dose aspirin is recommended to reduce the risk of MACE and MALE.7
After endovascular revascularization for PAD, dual antiplatelet therapy with a P2Y12 antagonist and low-dose aspirin is reasonable for at least 1 to 6 months.8-11

After endovascular or surgical revascularization in patients with PAD who require full-intensity anticoagulation for another indication and are not at high risk of bleeding, adding single antiplatelet therapy is reasonable.12,13
In patients with asymptomatic PAD, single antiplatelet therapy is reasonable to reduce the risk of MACE.
In patients with symptomatic PAD without recent revascularization, the benefit of dual antiplatelet therapy is uncertain.14,15
In patients with symptomatic PAD, the benefit of vorapaxar added to existing antiplatelet therapy is uncertain.16
After surgical revascularization for PAD with a prosthetic graft, dual antiplatelet therapy with a P2Y12 antagonist and low-dose aspirin may be reasonable for at least 1 month.17
In patients with PAD without another indication (eg, atrial fibrillation), full-intensity oral anticoagulation should not be used to reduce the risk of MACE and MALE.18-20

content.narrative_summary: Antiplatelet and antithrombotic therapies (eg, aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitors, dual antiplatelet therapy, low-dose rivaroxaban plus aspirin) are foundational in preventing myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, vascular death, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with symptomatic peripheral artery disease (PAD). The benefit of these agents in asymptomatic PAD is less certain due to higher bleeding risk. Evidence supports single antiplatelet therapy after revascularization to reduce recurrent symptoms and major adverse limb events (MALE), while more potent or dual antiplatelet regimens outside recent revascularization remain unproven and increase bleeding. Full-intensity anticoagulation without another indication (eg, atrial fibrillation) is not recommended. content.narrative_summary: The Synopsis emphasizes that cigarette smoking and other tobacco use are strong, dose-responsive risk factors for the development and progression of peripheral artery disease (PAD), including limb-related events and death. Quitting smoking is critical to reduce PAD risk and progression, with both pharmacological and behavioral strategies increasing cessation rates but remaining underutilized. content.title: 5.5. Diabetes Management for PAD
content.narrative_summary: Diabetes is a key risk factor for development and progression of PAD and CLTI. Guideline-based pharmacological and nonpharmacological interventions (including weight management) should be implemented in patients with diabetes and underlying PAD. Updated standards recommend use of glucagon-like peptide-1 agonists and SGLT-2 inhibitors to reduce MACE, and observational studies suggest adequate glycemic control improves outcomes, especially in CLTI. A coordinated diabetes care plan tailored to individual risk is essential. Randomized trials (LEADER, SUSTAIN-6, EMPA-REG, CANVAS, DECLARE-TIMI 58) demonstrated cardiovascular benefit with these agents.

section_headings: 5.6. Other Medical Therapies for Cardiovascular Risk Reduction in PAD
content.narrative_summary: This section reviews the role of diabetes management in PAD. SGLT2 inhibitor trials showed mixed results: CANVAS reported increased amputation risk with canagliflozin, not confirmed in subsequent studies, and subgroup analyses (EMPA-REG OUTCOME) demonstrated benefits leading to removal of the FDA black box warning; overall, RCT data and practice guidelines support SGLT2 inhibitors to reduce MACE in PAD with diabetes. Diabetes is associated with a 1.89–4.05-fold increased risk of PAD and higher rates of CLTI, MACE, and MALE; each 1% increase in hemoglobin A1c increases MACE risk by ~14%, underscoring the need for coordinated diabetes care including lifestyle, pharmacotherapy, and foot ulcer prevention. Poor glycemic control is a known risk factor for diabetic neuropathy, foot ulcers, and amputation; observational and registry studies link higher preprocedural and long-term hemoglobin A1c levels with increased amputation risk and worse outcomes after revascularization, supporting diabetes management as part of guideline-directed medical therapy for PAD.

content.narrative_summary: The synopsis states strong, high-quality, and consistent data support supervised exercise therapy (SET) to improve functional status, walking performance, and quality of life in chronic symptomatic PAD, including those being considered for or following revascularization. Coverage by Medicare and many insurers for SET is noted, with optimal delivery in clinic or hospital rehabilitation settings and potential third-party requirements. Randomized trials and meta-analyses demonstrate structured community- and home-based programs improve walking performance compared with usual care. Alternative nonwalking exercise forms also yield benefits. The recommendation-specific supportive text highlights RCT data showing persistent functional improvements with SET (including treadmill-based measures) lasting up to 7 years, although some measures such as the 6-minute walk test did not sustain gains at 6 months post-training.

content.title: 10. MANAGEMENT OF CLTI
content.narrative_summary: Femoropopliteal bypass using autogenous vein, generally the great saphenous vein, is preferred for surgical revascularization in patients with functionally limiting claudication due to femoropopliteal PAD, as autogenous conduits demonstrate superior patency compared with prosthetic grafts. Patients with chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI) manifest rest pain or tissue loss and benefit from team-based, multispecialty care centered on complete wound healing, infection management, pressure offloading, and revascularization to preserve functional limb and ambulatory status. Multidisciplinary teams may include expertise in vascular intervention, wound-healing therapies, podiatry, foot surgery, infection management, and cardiovascular risk reduction.

content.title: Recommendations for Pressure Offloading for CLTI
content.narrative_summary: Pressure offloading is a key component of CLTI management, reducing tissue loss and diabetic foot ulceration by mitigating shear, compressive, frictional, and tensile forces on the plantar foot. Specialist foot‐trained professionals assess anatomy, mechanics, and sensation to determine offloading interventions. High‐quality studies in diabetic patients demonstrate superiority of nonremovable devices over removable ones and show that customized footwear and orthoses reduce plantar ulcer recurrence when worn as prescribed. Limited data exist for non‐diabetic CLTI patients, although individualized offloading may still promote tissue growth and wound healing.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Pressure Offloading for CLTI

rows.recommendation: Patients with CLTI and diabetic foot ulcers should receive pressure offloading, when possible, to promote tissue growth and wound healing.1-9
Patients with PAD and previous diabetic foot ulcers should be referred for customized footwear that accommodates, protects, and fits the shape of their feet.10-12
Patients with CLTI and foot ulcers who do not have diabetes may be considered for pressure offloading to promote tissue growth and wound healing.

content.title: 10.3.2. Wound Care and Management of Infection for CLTI
section_headings: 10.3.2. Wound Care and Management of Infection for CLTI
content.narrative_summary: Management of infection and local wound care are critical for patients with chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI) and should be implemented concurrently with revascularization by a multispecialty team. Core components include prompt diagnosis, antibiotics, surgical debridement for abscess or necrotizing infection, minor amputation or reconstruction when needed, and negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT) for select cases. Adjunctive therapies such as hyperbaric oxygen have a limited role. After revascularization, coordinated multidisciplinary efforts with frequent wound assessment, various debridement techniques, tailored dressings to maintain a moist wound bed, and optimization of the wound-healing environment (smoking cessation, glycemic control, cardiovascular risk modification, nutrition) are recommended. Adjunctive biologic therapies may be considered for nonhealing wounds. To date, no RCTs or high-quality ...

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Wound Care and Management of Infection for CLTI

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with CLTI, prompt management of foot infection with antibiotics, debridement, and other surgical management is recommended.
2. In patients with CLTI with nonhealing wounds, wound care should be provided to optimize the wound-healing environment after revascularization with the goal of complete wound healing.
3. In patients with CLTI with nonhealing diabetic foot ulcers, hyperbaric oxygen therapy may be considered to assist in wound healing after revascularization.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues a discussion of wound-healing adjuncts in CLTI patients, noting limited data on NPWT, recent international consensus guidelines, and multiple RCTs and meta-analyses of hyperbaric oxygen therapy. content.narrative_summary: This section provides recommendations for the initial clinical evaluation and diagnostic approach to acute limb ischemia (ALI), noting that supporting studies are summarized in the Online Data Supplement.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the Initial Clinical Evaluation and Diagnostic Approach to ALI

rows.recommendation: 1. Patients with ALI should be evaluated on an emergency basis by a clinician with sufficient experience to assess limb viability and implement appropriate therapy.

2. In patients with suspected ALI, the initial clinical evaluation should rapidly assess limb viability and potential for salvage and can be achieved without noninvasive imaging (ie, duplex ultrasound, CTA, or MRA).1-6

3. In patients with ALI who have a complicated history of revascularization procedures, it may be reasonable to obtain noninvasive imaging (ie, duplex ultrasound, CTA, or MRA) before deciding to proceed with revascularization.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Revascularization for ALI

rows.recommendation: In patients with ALI and a salvageable limb, revascularization (endovascular or surgical, including catheter-directed thrombolysis) is indicated to prevent amputation.
In patients with ALI and a salvageable limb who are treated with catheter-directed thrombolysis, adjunctive revascularization (ie, endovascular or surgical) procedures can be useful.

In patients presenting with ALI from chemotherapeutic or prothrombotic viral states, it may be reasonable to take a more deliberate planning strategy before engaging in a definitive revascularization or medical treatment plan.
In patients with ALI with a nonsalvageable limb, revascularization of nonviable tissue should not be performed.

content.narrative_summary: This page summarizes the indication for revascularization in acute limb ischemia (ALI) with a salvageable limb to prevent irreversible tissue damage and amputation. It reviews both surgical thromboembolectomy and catheter-based thrombolysis (including ultrasound-accelerated, pharmacomechanical, and vacuum-assisted techniques) as effective therapies, with limb salvage rates exceeding 80% in many series. It emphasizes patient‐specific and anatomic factors, monitoring for compartment syndrome, and the need for definitive treatment of underlying lesions. Evidence from observational studies and randomized trials shows comparable limb salvage between open surgery and catheter‐directed thrombolysis but higher bleeding rates with thrombolysis. For bypass graft occlusions <14 days, catheter-directed thrombolysis may unmask lesions requiring further intervention. Longer occlusions typically necessitate other revascularization techniques. Additional evaluation is advised for ALI associated with proinflammatory or prothrombotic states (eg, cancer chemotherapy with platinum agents, tyrosine kinase inhibitors) and systemic illnesses such as COVID‐19. Further noninvasive imaging, stability assessment, and multidisciplinary discussion are recommended.

section_headings: 11.2.2. Adjunctive Therapies to Minimize Tissue Loss in ALI
content.narrative_summary: Patients presenting with ALI experience high rates of morbidity, mortality, and limb loss. Although timely revascularization is the goal, poor outcomes may be unavoidable, and adjuncts such as fasciotomy for compartment syndrome and early amputation may be necessary to minimize tissue loss and preserve limb function. Reperfusion injury arises from oxygen-free radical–mediated capillary leakage, leading to elevated compartment pressures, especially after prolonged ischemia; diagnosis relies on history, clinical findings, and compartment pressure measurements. Compartment syndrome is most common in the lower leg; prompt decompression interrupts progression to tissue necrosis. Recommendation-specific supportive text emphasizes the risk of reperfusion injury to ischemic muscles, the importance of monitoring and measuring compartment pressures, and the role of immediate fasciotomy based on clinical evidence to mitigate reperfusion sequelae.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Adjunctive Therapies to Minimize Tissue Loss in ALI

rows.recommendation: Patients with ALI should be monitored and treated for compartment syndrome with fasciotomy after revascularization (endovascular or surgical, including catheter-directed thrombolysis) to prevent the sequelae of reperfusion injury and need for amputation.
In patients with ALI with a threatened but salvageable limb (ie, category IIa or IIb), prophylactic fasciotomy is reasonable based on the clinical findings.

In patients with ALI and prolonged ischemia in whom revascularization (endovascular or surgical, including catheter-directed thrombolysis) is performed, concurrent and early amputation can be beneficial to avoid the morbidity of reperfusion.

content.title: 11.3. Diagnostic Evaluation for the Cause of ALI
section_headings: 11.3. Diagnostic Evaluation for the Cause of ALI
content.narrative_summary: ALI is a vascular emergency requiring rapid diagnosis and management, including timely revascularization. Underlying causes include native vessel or bypass graft thrombosis, arterial embolism, dissection, trauma, and associations such as COVID-19 infection. Determination of the cause is crucial to prevent recurrent events but should not delay limb-saving therapies. A detailed history and systems review should target known PAD, prior revascularization, atrial fibrillation or intracardiac thrombus, valvular or aortic disease, hypercoagulable states, vascular access history, current medications including anticoagulants, and family history of thrombosis.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for Diagnostic Evaluation for the Cause of ALI

rows.recommendation: 1. In patients with ALI, a comprehensive medical history and physical examination should be performed to determine the cause of thrombosis or embolization.
2. In patients with ALI, testing for a cardiovascular cause of thromboembolism can be useful.
